name: PDO nose thread lift

lead: A PDO nose thread lift is a minimally invasive, non-surgical rhinoplasty in which absorbable polydioxanone threads are inserted under the skin of the nose, sometimes together with filler, to raise the bridge or tip. People use it for a temporary reshaping with the lift visible soon after treatment.
Published literature is sparse: a 2024 review of clinical cases in Skin Research and Technology and one small registered trial of 10 people.

paras: Absorbable threads are placed under the skin to add support and volume, and the result lasts only as long as the threads take to absorb. It is promoted as an alternative to surgery for people who want a reversible change.
A 2024 review discusses adverse effects of nose thread procedures and prevention methods. The result is temporary as the threads absorb. It is performed by trained clinicians.

angle.text: PDO thread lifts are promoted as a non-surgical way to raise the nasal bridge or tip, sometimes combined with filler, with the lift visible soon after treatment. Absorbable threads under the skin add support, and the result is temporary as they absorb. Published evidence is limited to a case-based review and a small trial.

lead: A PDO nose thread lift is a minimally invasive, non-surgical rhinoplasty procedure in which absorbable polydioxanone (PDO) threads are inserted under the skin of the nose, sometimes together with filler, to raise the bridge or tip.[1]
Published literature is sparse: a 2024 review of clinical cases in Skin Research and Technology and one small registered trial.

paras: A 2024 review describes non-surgical rhinoplasty using absorbable "volumizing threads" combined with fillers, and explores whether this gives more precise nasal contouring than filler alone.[1]
The same review examines adverse effects of nose thread procedures through clinical cases and discusses methods of preventing them.[1]
A small registered trial of non-surgical rhinoplasty with PDO threads (n=10) was completed in 2021; results were not reviewed.[2] The main published source is the 2024 case-based review.[1]
